item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E001","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CONEVAL documented that the program had near-national geographic coverage, serving 444,585 young people in 2020; 63.47% received training certificates against a 63.25% target, and coverage reached 111.15% of the annual target. It provided scholarships, medical insurance, and training certificates, and prohibited political-electoral proselytism among training activities.","notes":["The excerpt states presence in 99.9% of municipalities, not literally nationwide operation."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E002","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":["The excerpt consistently presents these claims as allegations or criticism by Senator Kenia López Rabadán."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E003","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CONEVAL reported that national labor poverty fell from 40.3% to 38.5% between the fourth quarters of 2021 and 2022, while real per-capita labor income rose 4.3% and employment increased by 1.7 million. Rural and urban labor poverty both declined, but the 2022 national rate remained above the first-quarter 2020 level; men’s labor income was approximately 1.3 times women’s, and urban per-capita income was approximately twice rural income.","notes":["The excerpt says men earned approximately 1.3 times women’s income, not that women earned 1.3 times less than men."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E004","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"INEGI reported preliminary real GDP growth of 3.3% nationally in 2023, with growth in 30 of 32 states; Quintana Roo, San Luis Potosí, and Oaxaca grew fastest, while Coahuila and Tamaulipas contracted. The release states that the information derives from the national accounts system and is updated using surveys, administrative records, and primary data.","notes":["The excerpt does not explicitly state that the listed inputs were multiple federal and state data sources."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E005","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"UN special procedures communicated allegations of repeated killings of civilians by military or National Guard personnel in Nuevo Laredo and alleged delayed, non-transparent, partial, or military-led investigations, scene manipulation, intimidation of victims’ associates, and impunity. The communication notes that on 7 June 2023 AMLO stated an investigation had begun and that responsible personnel were about to be transferred to competent authorities; SEDENA later announced 16 military arrests and proceedings, while the communication stated that there was no record of competent civilian authorities participating in the investigation.","notes":["The excerpt uses the formulation that there was no record of civilian-authority participation; it does not use the broader phrase 'found no evidence.'"]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E006","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E007","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E008","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E009","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E010","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"UNAM’s IISUE described a 2024 edited volume analyzing AMLO-era education policy, including reform, financing, management, the Nueva Escuela Mexicana, Universities for Wellbeing, scholarships, disability inclusion, teacher formation, curriculum, higher education, science, technology, and AI legislation. The catalog presents it as a multidisciplinary, research-based analysis of advances, limitations, impacts, and challenges of current education policies.","notes":["The excerpt supports challenges and unresolved agenda items, but not the exact characterization 'unresolved challenges' as a standalone finding."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E011","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"During a September 2023 visit invited by Mexico, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention reported full and unimpeded access and acknowledged reforms including the accusatory criminal justice model, a National Registry of Detentions, restrictions on military jurisdiction, and releases. It nevertheless stated that arbitrary detention remained widespread, citing mandatory pre-trial detention, militarized policing linked to violence and torture, unresolved complaints, excessive arrest violence, deficient records, pressure on judges, weak public defense, poor detention conditions, prolonged migrant and child detention contrary to stated legal limits, discrimination against indigenous people, and negligible treatment for people with psychosocial disabilities.","notes":["The excerpt specifically describes child detention as contrary to legal restrictions and migrant detention beyond stated limits; 'unlawful migrant and child detention' was narrowed."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E012","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The UN Working Group reported that Mexico invited its September 2023 visit, provided full and unimpeded access, and had adopted reforms including an accusatory justice model, a detention registry, civilian jurisdiction for crimes against civilians, and releases. The same preliminary findings stated that arbitrary detention remained widespread, citing mandatory pre-trial detention, militarized policing associated with violence and torture, unresolved complaints, deficient arrest records, executive pressure on judges, weak legal assistance, abusive detention conditions, prolonged migrant and child detention contrary to stated legal limits, discrimination against indigenous people, and negligible treatment for people with psychosocial disabilities.","notes":["The excerpt specifically describes child detention as contrary to legal restrictions and migrant detention beyond stated limits; 'unlawful migrant and child detention' was narrowed."]}]}
